slides.body: In one sentence: Git never deletes an object that something still names, it keeps a private log of every name that recently changed, and it waits before deleting what nothing names.

slides.caption: Before the layers comes a precondition: was the work ever an object?

slides.direction: The table "Form of the work" from section 13.2. Committed: yes, a commit, trees and blobs, named by a branch or HEAD and the reflog. Stashed: yes, two or three commits, named by `refs/stash` and its reflog. Staged with `git add` and not committed: yes, a blob, named only by the index entry. Saved in the working tree and never staged: no object. Untracked or ignored: no object.

items: Looking in the reflog for an edit that was never committed. Root cause: a reflog records movements of refs only; edits to files, staging and unstaging leave no entry.
Counting positions in the HEAD reflog to find where a branch was. Root cause: HEAD has one line per step, including every step of a rebase; the branch reflog has one line per operation.

Writing main@{1} in an incident note. Root cause: a selector is relative to the log at that moment; it means something else after the next command and nothing on a colleague's machine. Record the full ID.
Asking a teammate or the server for "your reflog". Root cause: reflogs are never pushed or cloned; each repository has its own.
Trusting a time selector in a fresh clone. Root cause: the log starts when the clone was made, and Git answers with the oldest value it knows, with a warning.

slides.body: Your turn. Do Exercise 12.1, Level 1, "Read a reflog before you need it", in exercises/m11-m15-investigation-recovery.md.

Work in labs/shell. Before you print any reflog, predict the number of lines in the HEAD reflog and in the branch reflog for the operations the exercise has you perform, and which lines will appear in one and not in the other.

params.title: Four layers of protection

beats.text: A reset points a branch at another commit, another saved snapshot, and the work after it seems to vanish. Your CTO asks you two questions, and neither of them is "which command do we type". The first is: can we get it back? The second is: how sure are you, and how long do we have?
beats.tele: A reset points a branch at another commit, another saved snapshot, and the work after it seems to vanish. Your CTO asks you two questions, and neither of them is "which command do we type". The first is: can we get it back? The second is: how sure are you, and how long do we have?

beats.text: Both questions have exact answers. They depend on three facts about the lost work. Was it ever written into the object database, Git's store of everything it has saved? Does anything still name it? Has the clock run out? If you can answer those three from evidence, you can answer the CTO in a minute, and you can also say the harder sentence when it's true: this can't be recovered, and here is exactly why. Hold on to 18:40. We come back to it.
beats.tele: Both questions have exact answers. They depend on three facts about the lost work. Was it ever written into the object database, Git's store of everything it has saved? Does anything still name it? Has the clock run out? If you can answer those three from evidence, you can answer the CTO in a minute, and you can also say the harder sentence when it's true: this can't be recovered, and here is exactly why. Hold on to 18:40. We come back to it.

beats.text: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. This video opens the recovery module. For the next seven videos you take fifteen kinds of accident and bring the work back, or prove that it is gone.
beats.tele: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. This video opens the recovery module. For the next seven videos you take fifteen kinds of accident and bring the work back, or prove that it is gone.

beats.text: Three earlier videos supply the foundations. You know reachability: an object is kept as long as some starting point reaches it. You know what git reset --hard destroys. And you know force pushes and remote-tracking refs, your records of where a server's branches were. Today those pieces become a map, four layers of protection, and you learn to read the instrument you'll use in almost every recovery: the reflog.
beats.tele: Three earlier videos supply the foundations. You know reachability: an object is kept as long as some starting point reaches it. You know what `git reset --hard` destroys. And you know force pushes and remote-tracking refs, your records of where a server's branches were. Today those pieces become a map, four layers of protection, and you learn to read the instrument you'll use in almost every recovery: the reflog.

beats.text: explain how an unreachable commit survives a maintenance run.
beats.tele: explain how an unreachable commit survives a maintenance run.

beats.text: In one sentence: Git never deletes an object that something still names, it keeps a private log of every name that recently changed, and it waits before deleting what nothing names. Work is lost only when it was never an object, or when all of these protections are gone.
beats.tele: In one sentence: Git never deletes an object that something still names, it keeps a private log of every name that recently changed, and it waits before deleting what nothing names. Work is lost only when it was never an object, or when all of these protections are gone.

beats.text: Precisely. An object is kept as long as it is reachable from a starting point. The manual of git gc lists the starting points: branches and tags, the index, which is your proposed next commit, remote-tracking branches, reflogs, "and anything else in the refs/* namespace".
beats.tele: Precisely. An object is kept as long as it is reachable from a starting point. The manual of `git gc` lists the starting points: branches and tags, the index, which is your proposed next commit, remote-tracking branches, reflogs, "and anything else in the refs/* namespace".

beats.text: It adds one exclusion: a note attached to an object doesn't keep it alive. An object that no starting point reaches is unreachable. It still exists until a collection, Git's clean-up of its store, deletes it, and a collection deletes only objects older than a cut-off, two weeks by default.
beats.tele: It adds one exclusion: a note attached to an object doesn't keep it alive. An object that no starting point reaches is unreachable. It still exists until a collection, Git's clean-up of its store, deletes it, and a collection deletes only objects older than a cut-off, two weeks by default.

beats.text: That gives four layers, and a recovery is always a move from a lower layer back to the first one.
beats.tele: That gives four layers, and a recovery is always a move from a lower layer back to the first one.

beats.text: Layer one is refs, the names that hold an object ID. A branch, a tag, a remote-tracking ref, refs/stash, HEAD or the index names the object. It lasts until the ref is moved or deleted. You find it with git log --all or git for-each-ref.
beats.tele: Layer one is refs, the names that hold an object ID. A branch, a tag, a remote-tracking ref, `refs/stash`, HEAD or the index names the object. It lasts until the ref is moved or deleted. You find it with `git log --all` or `git for-each-ref`.

beats.text: Layer two is reflogs. A reflog entry names the object. The manual's defaults are 90 days, or 30 days for entries off the current history. The lab configuration overrides both, so that the transcripts don't depend on the day they were produced. You get the details in the next video. You find these with git reflog and git log -g.
beats.tele: Layer two is reflogs. A reflog entry names the object. The manual's defaults are 90 days, or 30 days for entries off the current history. The lab configuration overrides both, so that the transcripts don't depend on the day they were produced. You get the details in the next video. You find these with `git reflog` and `git log -g`.

beats.text: Layer three is the grace period. Nothing names the object, but its file is younger than the prune cut-off. Two weeks from the time the object was written, and then until the next collection runs. The tool is git fsck.
beats.tele: Layer three is the grace period. Nothing names the object, but its file is younger than the prune cut-off. Two weeks from the time the object was written, and then until the next collection runs. The tool is `git fsck`.

beats.text: Layer four is other repositories: another clone, the server, a bundle file, a backup. Its lifetime is independent of this repository.
beats.tele: Layer four is other repositories: another clone, the server, a bundle file, a backup. Its lifetime is independent of this repository.

beats.text: Before the layers comes a precondition: was the work ever an object?
beats.tele: Before the layers comes a precondition: was the work ever an object?

beats.text: Read the middle column. Committed, stashed, or staged with git add: an object exists. Saved in the working tree and never staged, or untracked: no object, and nothing for Git to bring back.
beats.tele: Read the middle column. Committed, stashed, or staged with `git add`: an object exists. Saved in the working tree and never staged, or untracked: no object, and nothing for Git to bring back.

beats.text: Now the reflog. In one sentence: a reflog is a local, append-only list of the values a ref has had, with the time, the person and the command behind each change, and every one of those old values is a name you can use.
beats.tele: Now the reflog. In one sentence: a reflog is a local, append-only list of the values a ref has had, with the time, the person and the command behind each change, and every one of those old values is a name you can use.

beats.text: Precisely. There's one reflog per ref that has logging enabled, plus one for HEAD. In a repository with a working tree, Git by default logs HEAD, branches, remote-tracking branches and notes refs. Tags get no reflog unless the setting core.logAllRefUpdates is always. Each entry stores the value before the change, the value after it, the committer identity and time, and a message written by the command.
beats.tele: Precisely. There's one reflog per ref that has logging enabled, plus one for HEAD. In a repository with a working tree, Git by default logs HEAD, branches, remote-tracking branches and notes refs. Tags get no reflog unless the setting `core.logAllRefUpdates` is `always`. Each entry stores the value before the change, the value after it, the committer identity and time, and a message written by the command.

beats.text: There are two kinds, and they answer different questions. The HEAD reflog records every movement of HEAD: commits, switches, resets, each step of a rebase, merges, cherry-picks. It answers "what did I do, in order", and it's the only log that sees detached HEAD, when you're on no branch. A branch reflog records only changes of that branch's value. It answers "where was this branch before the operation". A whole rebase is one entry there.
beats.tele: There are two kinds, and they answer different questions. The HEAD reflog records every movement of HEAD: commits, switches, resets, each step of a rebase, merges, cherry-picks. It answers "what did I do, in order", and it's the only log that sees detached HEAD, when you're on no branch. A branch reflog records only changes of that branch's value. It answers "where was this branch before the operation". A whole rebase is one entry there.

beats.text: When the reflog can't help: it records movements of refs only. Edits to files, staging and unstaging leave no entry. And it's local. No other clone and no server sees your reflog.
beats.tele: When the reflog can't help: it records movements of refs only. Edits to files, staging and unstaging leave no entry. And it's local. No other clone and no server sees your reflog.

beats.text: The textbook's analogy for the layers is a bank vault with a ledger. The safe-deposit boxes are objects. The index cards at the front desk are refs: each card names one box. When a card is rewritten, the clerk notes the old box number in a ledger, the reflog. Boxes that no card and no ledger line mentions are emptied in a periodic clear-out, but only boxes that have been untouched for two weeks.
beats.tele: The textbook's analogy for the layers is a bank vault with a ledger. The safe-deposit boxes are objects. The index cards at the front desk are refs: each card names one box. When a card is rewritten, the clerk notes the old box number in a ledger, the reflog. Boxes that no card and no ledger line mentions are emptied in a periodic clear-out, but only boxes that have been untouched for two weeks.

beats.text: The analogy breaks in two places. A box in Git also holds the numbers of older boxes: a commit names its parents and its tree. So one card protects a whole chain. And the ledger is private to one branch office: no other clone, and no server, sees your reflog.
beats.tele: The analogy breaks in two places. A box in Git also holds the numbers of older boxes: a commit names its parents and its tree. So one card protects a whole chain. And the ledger is private to one branch office: no other clone, and no server, sees your reflog.

beats.text: For the reflog alone, the textbook offers the "undo history" of an editor, kept per document. That breaks in two places too. A reflog has no undo command: it gives you old positions, and you decide what to do with them. And it records movements of refs only.

beats.text: In layer one the branch names da62b60, and through it every parent, tree and blob. In layer two a reflog entry names dbe6ec8, a commit that was removed from its branch. In layer three nothing names the object at all. Layer four is outside this .git.
beats.tele: In layer one the branch names `da62b60`, and through it every parent, tree and blob. In layer two a reflog entry names `dbe6ec8`, a commit that was removed from its branch. In layer three nothing names the object at all. Layer four is outside this `.git`.

beats.text: The ref itself holds only the new value. Each of the two log files gains one line with the old value and the new one. A command that moves the current branch appends to both files.
beats.tele: The ref itself holds only the new value. Each of the two log files gains one line with the old value and the new one. A command that moves the current branch appends to both files.

beats.text: git gc --prune=now is also 🔴 DANGEROUS: a collection with no grace period at all. Before it runs, the five answers. What it changes: it packs objects and deletes unreachable ones immediately. What it can destroy: everything on layer three. How to preview: git prune -n lists what an immediate prune would delete. How to recover: from another repository only. When it's appropriate: you'll see in the last video of this module. Here the preview is the point.

How to recover: from another repository only. When it's appropriate: you'll see in the last video of this module. Here the preview is the point.

beats.tele: Predict: the commit `dbe6ec8` is on no branch. Does it survive? Say it out loud. I'll wait.

beats.text: It survives. git prune -n prints nothing: nothing would be deleted. After the collection, git cat-file -t still answers commit. All twelve objects were packed, the lost commit included.
beats.tele: It survives. `git prune -n` prints nothing: nothing would be deleted. After the collection, `git cat-file -t` still answers `commit`. All twelve objects were packed, the lost commit included.

beats.text: The reflog entry HEAD@{1} names it, so it's on layer two, and a reflog is a starting point for reachability.
beats.tele: The reflog entry `HEAD@{1}` names it, so it's on layer two, and a reflog is a starting point for reachability.

beats.text: Nine. Read it from the bottom. Each line is "the value HEAD had after this event". HEAD@{0} is always the current value. The amend at HEAD@{3} replaced 14a18d6 with f1f247e, and the old commit is still listed one line below. The two checkout lines record branch switches, which change HEAD and no branch.

beats.text: The reflog of main has five lines where HEAD has nine: the switches and the work on the other branch are absent. git reflog list, which needs Git 2.45 or later, names every ref that has a log.

beats.text: A reflog entry is addressed with a selector, and a selector is a revision, a way of naming a commit, that every command accepts.
beats.tele: A reflog entry is addressed with a selector, and a selector is a revision, a way of naming a commit, that every command accepts.

beats.text: HEAD@{1} is the value HEAD had one change ago. @{1} with no name is for the current branch, not for HEAD. @{-1} is different in kind: it's the branch that was checked out before the current one, a name and not a position. Quote selectors in the shell, because braces are special to some shells.

Quote selectors in the shell, because braces are special to some shells.

beats.text: Time-based selectors read the timestamps in the log. Predict the last command: the log began on 7 September. What does "two days ago" return? Quick quiz, three options: an error, nothing at all, or the oldest value Git knows. Say it out loud.

beats.text: At 10:10:30 main was still at da62b60, because the merge happened at 10:12. The last command asks for a time before the log begins. Option three: Git answers with the oldest value it knows, 538ea2f, and says so in a warning. A time selector is a statement about your local log, never about the project. In a clone made today, main@{1.week.ago} can't know where main was a week ago.

beats.text: git log -g walks a reflog instead of the ancestry, with placeholders for the reflog fields.
beats.tele: `git log -g` walks a reflog instead of the ancestry, with placeholders for the reflog fields.

beats.text: %gd is the selector, %gs the reflog message, %gn the name of the person who made the change. --grep-reflog filters by reflog message. The third command lists only the entries that created commits. That's how you search a long log for the event you need, instead of counting positions.

beats.text: Last, the files.
beats.tele: Last, the files.

beats.text: One event on the current branch is two lines, one in each file. The first ID of a line is the old value and the second the new one. That's more than git reflog prints, and it matters: the old value of the newest line tells you where a ref was even when no older line exists.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Looking in the reflog for an edit that was never committed. Root cause: a reflog records movements of refs only; edits to files, staging and unstaging leave no entry.
beats.tele: Looking in the reflog for an edit that was never committed. Root cause: a reflog records movements of refs only; edits to files, staging and unstaging leave no entry.

beats.text: Counting positions in the HEAD reflog to find where a branch was. Root cause: HEAD has one line per step, including every step of a rebase; the branch reflog has one line per operation.
beats.tele: Counting positions in the HEAD reflog to find where a branch was. Root cause: HEAD has one line per step, including every step of a rebase; the branch reflog has one line per operation.

beats.text: Writing main@{1} in an incident note. Root cause: a selector is relative to the log at that moment; it means something else after the next command and nothing on a colleague's machine. Record the full ID.
beats.tele: Writing `main@{1}` in an incident note. Root cause: a selector is relative to the log at that moment; it means something else after the next command and nothing on a colleague's machine. Record the full ID.

beats.text: Asking a teammate or the server for "your reflog". Root cause: reflogs are never pushed or cloned; each repository has its own.
beats.tele: Asking a teammate or the server for "your reflog". Root cause: reflogs are never pushed or cloned; each repository has its own.

beats.text: Trusting a time selector in a fresh clone. Root cause: the log starts when the clone was made, and Git answers with the oldest value it knows, with a warning.
beats.tele: Trusting a time selector in a fresh clone. Root cause: the log starts when the clone was made, and Git answers with the oldest value it knows, with a warning.

"Three days of commits on a feature branch, and I reset the branch" is layer two: the branch reflog has the old tip, and with default settings the entry for a commit off the current history lives for 30 days. You tell the CTO: recoverable, high confidence, weeks of margin, and nobody should run maintenance in that clone meanwhile.

beats.text: A strong answer defines the reflog by what it records and where it lives, then connects it to reachability: why an entry keeps a commit alive through a collection. It distinguishes the HEAD reflog from a branch reflog and says which one you read for which incident. It states the limits without being asked: local only, movements of refs only, entries that expire, and the cases in which there is no reflog. And it finishes with a concrete recovery in two steps: find the ID, then give it a name.

beats.text: Work is protected by refs, then by reflogs, then by a grace period, then by other repositories; a recovery moves it back to a ref.
beats.tele: Work is protected by refs, then by reflogs, then by a grace period, then by other repositories; a recovery moves it back to a ref.

beats.text: Only work that became an object can be recovered from Git: committed, stashed, or staged.
beats.tele: Only work that became an object can be recovered from Git: committed, stashed, or staged.

beats.text: A reflog entry holds an old value, a new value, who, when and which command; every old value is a usable name.
